Because KeyBank refused to recognize me as an heir/successor in interest to my father 's estate, KeyBank refused to discuss the mortgage account with me and refused to readily accept payments from me. Despite refusing to accept money from me, KeyBank 's collection department called continuously for years, but always asked to speak to my father, even though they had express knowledge he was deceased. This was a terrible emotional stress on myself and his sister, the executrix, so much so that she could not handle the stress any longer, and wrote to KeyBank advising them to discuss this matter with me only. KeyBank refused that request and still continued to contact my aunt ( executrix ). 
Eventually, both my aunt and I wrote to KeyBank and complained of their refusal to discuss the mortgage with me. One of their lawyers reached out and informed me that we needed to fill out a particular form- which I believe we had already submitted - in order for KeyBank to discuss the mortgage account. Nonetheless, we filled the form out ( again ), submitted it, and received written confirmation that it had been received AND that, going forward, I would be able to make payments on the mortgage account and discuss the mortgage with KeyBank. Unfortunately, that never happened. Despite repeated promises and assurances from KeyBank representatives and lawyers, I was never given authorization to pay on the account or be able to discuss the account with Keybank. I was able to make a payment by phone once ( it took almost an hour ) but after that, the next time I called, I was informed they saw no record of me in the system that would allow them to discuss the matter with me. 
I continued to have difficulty making payments and Keybank filed a foreclosure action. I filed an Answer and Counterclaim. The judge allowed KeyBank to obtain discovery from me, but refused on multiple occasions to allow me to obtain discovery from KeyBank, even though I explained to him that the evidence I sought, including the telephone recordings, would refute the foreclosure claims as well as support my defenses and counterclaims. That failure by the Court toallow me discovery resulted in KeyBank receiving summary judgment. They then, despite pending appeals, rushed to sell the house as quickly as possible.

Just prior to the grant of summary judgment, and because I was not being treated fairly by the state court, we filed a Federal court case in OH, alleging violations of RESPA, TILA FDCPA and various state law breach of contract claims. That case is still pending. 
The house was sold at auction on XX/XX/XXXX, despite every effort I made to pay off the mortgage in full and despite efforts to stay the proceedings. 
It is my belief that KeyBank and its law firms, acted in concert in order to keep their unethical and illegal actions under wraps. Keybank and its lawyers filed affidavits and other pleadings containing false statements. By way of example, claiming that I had missed a XXXX, XXXX payment. The foreclosure law firm, XXXX XXXX, XXXX and Key Bank both have possession of evidence contrary to what was filed, and they withheld that evidence in order to obtain a favorable ruling and get the house. For example, KeyBank and its law firms are in actual possession of the telephone recordings showing that I tried to make the required mortgage payments. I was told specifically by representatives of KeyBank that the foreclosure should not have been filed, but the law firms went forward anyway. Even as late as last year, my aunt, seeing that I was not getting a reasonable response from KeyBank, sent yet another letter explaining the problem and our desire to pay, but that letter was ignored completely. 
The house has been sold, and even though I am filing a XXXX XXXX, I may lose my ancestral home. 
It is my assertion that the foreclosure action was wrongfully brought, and that KeyBank and its representatives brought about the foreclosure themselves.

Those homeowners should contact their mortgage servicer who will evaluate them for one of FHA 's loss mitigation options.

If you have an FHA-insured mortgage, these options may be available to you.

Standalone Partial Claim : Allows mortgage payment arrearages to be placed in a zero-interest subordinate lien against the property. The Partial Claim amount does not require payment until the last mortgage payment is made, the loan is refinanced, or the property is sold, whichever occurs first.

FHA-HAMP Combination Loan Modification and Partial Claim : The FHA-HAMP Combination Loan Modification and Partial Claim establishes an affordable monthly payment, resolves the outstanding mortgage payment arrearages, and permanently modifies the first mortgage monthly payment. The Partial Claim is a zero-interest subordinate lien that will include a portion of the amount to be resolved and if you meet the requirements, a principal deferment. The remainder is added to the principal loan balance of your first mortgage and extends the term for 30 years ( 360 months ) at a fixed interest

Regulation X, implemented by the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau ( CFPB ) pursuant to the Real Estate Settlement Procedure Act ( RESPA ), governs the handling of mortgage servicing, including loss mitigation and foreclosure proceedings. It establishes certain rights and responsibilities for both borrowers and servicers, with the objective of promoting fair and transparent practices in the mortgage industry. RESPA supersedes state law via the Supremacy Clause of the United States. 

Section 1024.41 of Regulation X specifically addresses the procedures and requirements for evaluating and responding to borrowers loss mitigation applications. It stipulates that once a complete application is received, the servicer must acknowledge the receipt in writing within five business days. Furthermore, the servicer is required to exercise reasonable diligence in obtaining all necessary documents and evaluating the application for a loss mitigation option. During this review process, foreclosure proceedings, including the scheduling of an auction date must be stayed. 

These actions by SNSC SERVICING is the textbook scenario why Dual Track Foreclosure laws were enacted. To stop banks from selling a homeowners home while at the same time reviewing them for work out options. 

The failure to cancel the auction and to complete the short sale review directly contradicts the spirit and intent of Regulation X, which aims to provide homeowners with a fair opportunity to explore loss mitigation options before facing the dire consequences of a foreclosure auction.

( "" WF '' ). Further complicating the process of securing replacement coverage is the current perceived wildfire risk throughout Colorado, which has resulted in lack of available coverage from any carriers in more than 50 % of the state, including in the area in which our property is located. 

We received an initial notice of lack of evidence of insurance coverage from WF on XX/XX/XXXX stating, in part, "" Because hazard insurance is required on your property, we plan to buy insurance for your property '', clearly indicating that XXXX had not yet purchased such coverage. We bound replacement coverage effective XX/XX/XXXX and provided this information to Wells Fargo on XX/XX/XXXX. We received confirmation of receipt of proof of coverage from WF on XX/XX/XXXX, with additional commentary stating, in part, "" Our records show that there was a lapse in coverage from XX/XX/XXXX to XX/XX/XXXX. An insurance charge of {$2600.00} may be charged to your account for the period of time that the coverage was in force. In order to avoid this charge or have it reversed from your account; please provide us with evidence of insurance for this lapse period. '' On XX/XX/XXXX, we provided a No Loss Letter to WF which certifies that no losses occurred during the lapse period, memorializing the fact that there are no losses to insure against during the lapse period. 

Page 5, section 5, paragraph two of the LA states, in part, "" If Borrower fails to maintain any of the coverages described above, Lender may obtain insurance coverage, at Lender 's option and Borrower 's expense. "". As evidence of insurance was provided to WF on XX/XX/XXXX and subsequent correspondence from WF dated XX/XX/XXXX indicates that WF had not yet obtained coverage at Borrower 's expense, the above language in Section 5 of the LA should prohibit WF from obtaining coverage at Borrower 's expense "" after '' evidence of coverage has been provided. 

In addition to the foregoing, page 5, section 5, paragraph two of the LA further states "" Any amounts disbursed by Lender under this Section 5 shall become additional debt of Borrower secured by this Security Instrument. '' On XX/XX/XXXX, we received a copy of the declarations for an insurance policy "" purportedly '' taken out by WF. The declarations show an effective date of XX/XX/XXXX and an annual premium in the amount of {$46000.00}. The bottom right corner of the policy declarations notes a policy issue date of XX/XX/XXXX. There is no evidence of any amounts actually "" disbursed '' by WF as is required under the terms of the LA. 

Our latest mortgage statement, dated XX/XX/XXXX, now shows an escrow balance of ( {$2600.00} ), with interest being charged at 3.125 % per annum. As WF 's correspondence history and the declarations page for the policy which WF purportedly took out both clearly indicate that it did not obtain coverage until "" after '' we had provided evidence of coverage, WF has no exposure for the lapse period pursuant to the No Loss Letter provided to WF, and further WF has failed to provide proof of any amounts actually disbursed by WF, it is our position that WF has breached the terms of the LA on multiple points. We have attempted to discuss this matter with the appropriate personnel at WF via telephone on numerous occasions and have repeatedly been denied contact information for anyone in the department which administers the insurance coverage requirements under WF 's loan agreements. From my own perspective, I felt I was being rushed into this deal as soon as my son showed interest in getting the solar panel under false pretenses. It was solely the fault of Dividend Finance that decided to put only my name on the solar loan- which caused me to lose the $ XXXX tax credit. I filed the complaint initially to XXXX XXXX XXXX, and the VP reached out to Dividend Finance. The answer was because Dividend Finances company policy forbids co-signing, only one persons name can be on the loan. But they didnt want to answer how during the process only my name was chosen to be on the loan. There was no one - from Dividend Finance nor XXXX XXXX XXXX gave me the courtesy notice during the application or the final paperwork signing that there were changes in the loan application.Lack of transparency from both companies cost me the federal tax credit. In the end, Dividend Finance was the loan originator, and it is Dividend Finance, who was unyielding, refused to accept any responsibility and refused to propose any remedy. The answer from them was always the consistent NO and their stance on company policy. 


Additional Serious Issues There were further significant problems related to the solar panels and the associated loan. The installment team performed a Botched job on the electric wiring, but refused to rectify the problem. Consequently, the electric bill went skyrocket, particularly during the XXXX period following the initial installment. This resulted in my son incurring a significant higher bill from the electric company. The system failed to do what it promised once again! 

After numerous attempts to seek a resolution without success, we lodged a complaint against XXXX XXXX XXXX and Dividend Fiance. Instead of accepting responsibility, these two entities shifted blame onto each other, leaving us without a clear resolution. We didnt know what happened internally in these two companies during this tumultuous period ; however, XXXX XXXX XXXX fired several people, including XXXX XXXX XXXX of the XXXX  managers who was involved in handling my complaint. Ultimately, they refused to annul the contract, or acknowledge any wrongdoing. Had we chosen to return the equipment, we would have been responsible for all associated labor costs and fees. After losing federal tax credit, we could not shoulder further financial losses, forcing us into silence over this flawed and potentially unlawful transaction. 

We received misleading information regarding the loan 's nature and the solar panel 's efficacy. The sales representative employed deceitful tactics to secure the contract, a clear indication of dishonest business practices. Misled by incorrect information and advice, my son and I were unwittingly ensnared in a scheme that should never have occurred. 

Should Dividend Finance attempt to disclaim any association with these issues, it is imperative to recognize that XXXX XXXX XXXX acted as their contractor. Beyond receiving commissions from each new contract, Dividend Finance benefited from an additional XXXX loan, averaging $ XXXX in principal, which yielded interest payments over two decades. As the primary beneficiary of every contract, Dividend Finance should, therefore, assume a greater portion of the responsibility and liability for the ensuing problems. 


Dividend Finance Caused Further Problem During the Sales of House in XXXX When my son decided to sell his house equipped with solar panels, he accepted an offer from a modest, working-class family who were particularly fond of the property. The sales process was smooth until we encountered issues with Dividend Finance. Adhering to the company 's policies, we initially attempted to include the solar loan amount in the house 's selling price. However, the buyers encountered difficulties with their bank in increasing the pre-approved mortgage amount. Consequently, the alternative option explored was for the buyers to assume the solar loan separately from their mortgage. Despite their willingness and after submitting the necessary application to Dividend Finance, the transfer request was denied on the grounds that the potential buyers did not meet the qualification criteria. 

This outcome was perplexing, especially since the buyers had successfully passed all financial assessments through their realtor and the mortgage approval process. At this juncture, my son had already accepted their offer, and considerable investments had been made by both parties to finalize the sale, only to be obstructed by Dividend Finance 's refusal to facilitate the loan transfer. The buyers even proposed a temporary arrangement to make monthly payments directly to me, with a mutual agreement to reapply for the loan transfer once their financial situation improved. 


Dividend Finance Still Denied the Current Home Owners Application to Take over the Solar Loan in XXXX Fast forward to XXXX, the current homeowners re-applied for the loan transfer, only to face rejection from Dividend Finance for the same reasons cited previously. I engaged in multiple discussions with Dividend Finance seeking a viable solution for this unique scenario, suggesting various conventional methods such as securing a co-signer or placing a lien on the property. Nonetheless, Dividend Finance remained intractable, insisting on adherence to their company policy without exception. Consequently, I was notified that the outstanding solar loan balance of $ XXXX was my responsibility to settle, given the ongoing ineligibility of the current homeowners. 

Despite escalating the matter to Dividend Finance 's resolution teampurportedly the highest authority for case reviewtheir response was disappointingly predictable. The resolution team 's reluctance to deviate from their usual procedures left us with no alternative but to fulfill the demand to repay the remaining solar loan balance, further compounded by the property 's change in ownership and the new owners ' continued disqualification for the loan transfer.

Unreasonable and Unjust Company Policy : A Call for Federal Review Dividend Finance has consistently utilized its company policy as a shield for years, particularly through its rigid stance on loan applications and its staunch NO-Co-Signer policy. As a fintech company issuing loans for energy-efficient solutions and advocating for a green economy, Dividend Finance ought to utilize every lawful means to support the average XXXX 's pursuit of energy efficiency. Contrarily, the implementation of a NO-co-signer policy inflicts undue stress and harm on consumers, lacking a justifiable reason from the consumer 's perspective.

Given Dividend Finance 's involvement in providing solar panels and loans, the company inevitably intersects with the housing market and mortgage loans, becoming an integral participant in the sales process of houses. Transactions involving houses can become incredibly complex, imposing exhaustion on both parties involved. A company embedded in energy solutions should not become the impediment in such transactions. It is baffling that a solar loan lender could identify a disqualifying factor in their assessment that prevents a buyer, capable of affording a house with a mortgage, from securing a solar solution with a loan. Worse still, Dividend Finance has consistently declined to offer any form of accommodation to rectify such situations, making it the sole dissenting voice in these transactions. The company must immediately adopt a collaborative stance and integrate effectively within the broader industry.

Ownership of houses frequently extends to multiple individuals, similar to home mortgages. The allowance of co-signers for personal and car loans is common practice, with solar loans often paralleling mortgages. Yet, Dividend Finance has chosen to deviate from industry norms, crafting policies that exclusively benefit the lender at the expense of all other transactional parties. 

My four-year ordeal with Dividend Finance reveals a company indifferent to consumer grievances. The establishment of various departments purportedly addressing complaints resembles a mere spectacle, offering no substantive resolution and serving only to fulfill a legal obligation to provide a resolution service.

Dividend Finance must justify its stringent loan application policies to federal agencies, clarifying the necessity of such practices within this specific industry context, which undeniably impacts consumers negatively. While the company may argue that these policies streamline processes and mitigate default risks, efficiency can not be pursued solely for the lender 's benefit. Should Dividend Finance persist in its current practices without considering consumers or the broader implications, federal intervention becomes imperative to dictate appropriate conduct. 

Despite proclamations of environmental commitment and a "" customer-centric '' ethos, Dividend Finance 's actions betray a cold indifference towards those it purports to serve, focusing solely on securing monthly interest payments without concern for its impact. The company 's mission to "" improve the outcome for everyone involved '' rings hollow, resembling nothing more than a public relations facade.

The representative advised me not to make payments and to wait until the modification was complete. The representative said another reason I shouldn't make payments is because I wouldn't know what the new payments would be that would be set for me in the modification agreement. Moreover, much of the delay was because of the Mr. Cooper staff and now it seems I am stuck holding the bill.

Bank of America stated repeatedly in their opposition to complaint in bankruptcy on XX/XX/XXXX by attorney XXXX and later that my loan is a federally backed mortgage and that it was securitized by XXXX. 
It is settled ( relevant to federally backed mortgages ) that the applicable law is federal. In a decision that has become a leading case on the question, XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, arising under the National Housing Act, Title II, 12 U.S.C. 1707 ff. we held : But we do find it to be clear that the source of the law governing the relations between the United States and the parties to the mortgage here involved is federal. ( Citations omitted ) * * * It is therefore equally clear that if the law of the State of Washington is to have any application in the foreclosure proceeding it is not because it applies of its own force, but because either the Congress, the FHA, or the Federal Court adopts the local rule to further federal policy. 268 F.2d at 382.

The first question is whether the Congress adopted state law in its definition of mortgage and first mortgage. California argues that it did. The language relied upon appears in 12 U.S.C. 1736 ( a ), and reads : The term mortgage means a first mortgage on real estate, in fee simple. We rejected Californias argument in View Crest, supra, where identical language in 12 U.S.C. 1707 was relied upon. We said : The argument is that in adopting the state definition of first mortgage, Congress intended to adopt all the incidents of the mortgage relation under state law including remedies on default and the appointment of receivers. That this is not the case is clear from reading section 1713 of the same Act which defines certain acts as being in default ( part g ) and sets out certain remedies that the FHA can pursue such as institution of foreclosure ( part k ) proceedings without reference to whether or not there is such a remedy for the default described in the State where the property is located. Moreover, there is no apparent reason for assuming that Congress in incorporating by reference certain duties under state law also meant to restrict the United States to the state remedies for breach of those duties * * 268 F.2d at 382.

Therefore, Bank Of America can not foreclose nonjudicially under Alaska law when the mortgage is federally back mortgage.

Bank Of America recorded on XX/XX/XXXX a 6th noncompliant notice of default and sale for XX/XX/XXXX in blatant disregard to Congress and the federal courts that clearly determined that federally backed mortgages are under federal and not under state law unless Congress specifically adopted Alaska nonjudicial law, which Congress never did.

     Claims under TILA and RESPA can be raised against the owners and servicers of zombie second mortgages. Junior mortgages are not exempt from most of the important TILA and RESPA provisions, although some requirements do not apply to HELOC loans. 

     Both TILA and RESPA allow claims for statutory penalties, compensatory damages, and attorney fees. These laws also establish an important industry standardthat owners and servicers of mortgage loans must keep borrowers regularly informed about the status of their loans. Claims under TILA and RESPA can include:

	TILA transfer of loan ownership notices. Effective in XXXX, provisions of Regulation Z require that new owners or assignees of mortgage loans inform borrowers of a transfer of loan ownership within thirty days after a loan is sold. 12 C.F.R.  1026.39(b), implementing 15 U.S.C.  1641(g). Transfer of ownership notices must provide specific information that borrowers need to understand their current payment obligations. The failure to inform borrowers of sales of their loans contributes to the expectation that there is no need take action regarding an ongoing payment obligation. 

	RESPA notice of transfer of mortgage servicing rights. A transfer of servicing rights for a second mortgage triggers obligations under RESPA for both the transferor servicer and the transferee servicer to provide a timely notice to the borrower. 12 U.S.C.  2605(b); Reg. X 12 C.F.R.  1024.33(b). Failure to give timely notice deprives a borrower of another important tool for ascertaining the status of an account. 

	The TILA periodic statement requirements. Amendments to the TILA periodic statement rule were designed to prevent the surprise appearance of a long-dormant second mortgage together with unexpected claims for years of accrued interest and fees. See Reg. Z, 12 C.F.R.  1026.41, implementing 15 U.S.C.  1638(f). Under the rule, servicers must keep borrowers informed about the status of a second mortgage, including whether it has been charged-off or re-activated for collection, as well as who currently owns the loan and how to contact appropriate parties for up-to-date information. The rule requires heightened periodic statement disclosures when the loan is in arrears. The initial version of this periodic statement rule went into effect in XXXX XXXX. Amendments effective in XXXX XXXX added requirements for disclosing the charged-off status of a loan and for giving notice before collection on a charged-off loan resumed. 12 C.F.R.  1026.41(e)(6). The amended rule bars collection of interest and fees that a lender alleges accrued after the lender gave notice of charge-off and before it gave notice of resumption of payments. 12 C.F.R.  1026.41(e)(6)(ii)(B).

	TILA rescission. A successful TILA rescission voids a lenders security interest in the borrowers real property, effectively barring a foreclosure.

Consumer complaint narrative:
My husband and I bought a new home in XX/XX/XXXX. It was a brand new community and we knew the house would not be ready until XX/XX/XXXX. 

We are XXXX XXXX  that were relocated to XXXX XXXX NV for my husband 's work. It is important to note that this is our first time buying a house in the United States and the buying process is very different in XXXX. Over the next year we travelled to XXXX XXXX a few times to see the house and to make our selections. We sold our home in XXXX in order to invest our profits as a down payment on our home in XXXX XXXX. It was always clear that even though we were on a temporary visa that allowed us to be in the US, we were permanently relocating with our young children. 

We were referred to a lender by the builder which we worked with. Throughout the purchasing process we were asked to complete numerous different forms in order to qualify for a mortgage and to provide a gamete of documents as proof of funds. At the beginning of the process, we were asked to complete a Uniform Residential Loan Application ( URLA ). Months went by as the house was being built. I spoke to our lender in XX/XX/XXXX where I asked numerous questions about the lending process. XXXX of the questions I asked was about refinancing our mortgage as we were purchasing our home at a time when rates were quite high. The lender confirmed that there are no penalties for refinancing. *I have my personal handwritten notes from this call. 

Over the summer of XXXX we sold our home in XXXX, packed up our belongings and were ready to move to our new home. Once our home was officially sold in XXXX we were asked to provide proof of funds as well as confirmation of our final numbers ; which we provided. Keeping in mind that the profits from the sale of our home had to be converted to US dollars as well as wired to our US account. We provided all documents that were requested and had sufficient funds to close on the house. Our closing date was set for XX/XX/XXXX. 

We asked our lender when we would know our final numbers for our monthly mortgage payments. We were told that we would only know the final numbers once we sign at the title company. It is important to note that we do not know the process of buying a home in the US and nothing was explained to us. We asked what a title company was, what did escrow mean, and numerous questions around insurance. We also asked why we needed an appraisal, everything was new for us. Finally on XX/XX/XXXX I received a text message from our lender that we would be receiving a XXXX of the last disclosures. Upon reviewing these documents I texted the lender advising that the dates on the document were not correct and asked when we would be going over the numbers ( monthly payments, fees, insurance ect. ) We were told the date can be changed if funding goes smoothly and that we need to sign the documents due to a 3 day recission period and that if we were trying to close on time for the XXXX, they need the signed documents asap. We felt pressured to sign the documents right away as we were living in a hotel with our kids and dog waiting to move to our new home. We were still asking at this point when we would be receiving information about our home insurance, and asking how much the insurance was going to cost. We were never explained any of the financial numbers, we were told by the lender that all this would be done at the signing at the title company. Regarding our insurance the text message said that our insurance policy was done as an investment property due to our type of loan and that as soon as we close they would email the insurance agent to have him change it to a primary. I confirmed by text again that once we close this would be changed to primary and asked if we needed mortgage insurance. We were asking these questions the day before we were to sign at the title company, clearly feeling uninformed. We later discovered that we were sold tenant insurance! 

The lender asked us on XX/XX/XXXX by email to print, sign and date the Intent to Proceed with the date of : XX/XX/XXXX and return it to them as they had received the wrong form from the investor as they were supposed to have been sent XXXX in the initial disclosures in XX/XX/XXXX. This is another example of the lender not being honest and not acting in our best interests. 

The next day, on XX/XX/XXXX we arrived for our appointment at the title company. We are anxious for numerous reasons but also because we wanted to understand our numbers. As we were signing document after document I told my husband, I don't even know what we're signing. I asked the person who was having us sign the documents why the documents say that this is an investment property and I asked them when we would be getting to the final numbers and when they would be explaining the numbers to us. They informed us that this is not done at title and that that is done with our lender and that we could call them if we wanted to. We called them and they were on the phone so we texted them and asked them why our property is documented as an investment property when this is not an investment property, this is our primary home. We received a text back stating that this is the type of loan we had to get in order to have us approved and that they used the rental income to offset the mortgage to qualify. It was either that or a foreign national with a foreign national rate so both are done as investment properties. I then replied asking what rental income? They responded with the market rental income from appraisal. At this point, we were signing documents we clearly had never been explained, we had no idea what was going on and I was physically not feeling well because we did not understand what was going on. This was never an investment, this was and still is our primary home. We never had any intentions on purchasing this home for an investment. When we had seen the term investment in the documents prior to arriving at the title company we thought the term 'investment ' was referred to as home ownership in the US - an investment. We did not realize that this was a type of loan or loan program. 

XX/XX/XXXX was our closing date. We found out that afternoon that we would not be able to close from the builder. Our lender never told us! We reached out to them and asked when they were going to tell us we were not closing that day and they apologized as they were in training and did not have access to their phone.

Our property is registered with the county treasurer as our primary home, we signed a document at closing from our HOA confirming that this was our primary home and that we would be living there and we told our lender that this was our primary home and confirmed this on our URLA. 

About a month ago we started to look into refinancing our mortgage as we have a very high interest rate. As we were about to have our mortgage paid by a new lender, we were advised that there was a prepayment penalty of {$18000.00}. We had no idea there was a penalty as we had been told there was not going to be one. Due to our current loan we have a prepayment penalty if we want to refinance within the next 3 years! 

On XX/XX/XXXX I called the investor in order to confirm the prepayment penalty as this was the first time I was hearing of this. I asked them how this was possible and that we were needing to refinance to a better interest rate. They advised that it was not likely possible for me to get a better rate in this market. I advised them that I had secured a better rate of 1.75 % less than what we currently have. I was told that I should jump on it then ; which is a horrible thing to tell someone that you just confirmed to that they are locked into an {$18000.00} prepayment penalty. 

We have since sent an email on XX/XX/XXXX requesting our initial disclosures and loan application and followed up on XX/XX/XXXX and have still never received a response. 

It is clear that we were never explained anything about our loan or the loan program, we never once met with our lender. We were taken advantage of because we are foreign and no due diligence was done with our loan. Above our prepayment penalty we incurred additional expenses on our home appraisal as there was a need for extra forms to compare rental income in the area. 

We do not feel that the lender or the investor did their due diligence on our file and we were taken advantage of and put into a terrible situation. No one reviewed our file for accuracy or compliance. This is a clear case of occupancy fraud. Our lender knew beyond a shadow of a doubt that this was our primary home, NOT an investment property. They then locked us into a program for an investment property with a massive prepayment penalty. We were put in a predatory lending situation as we asked for explanations of costs and our insurance numerous times which were met with silence. 

I have text messages as well as emails and documents to confirm everything that I have mentioned in my complaint is factual. A prepayment penalty of over XXXX XXXX dollars is a massive financial hardship to have to pay off just to refinance to a lower rate. The lender was aware that we would be refinancing as soon as we could due to our high interest rate. We were not treated fairly or responsibly by the lender or the investor. 

We are concerned on how to approach this situation because of not knowing the lending process we also do not know how to complaint process works. We are simply looking for assistance and a friend referred us to CFPB because the lender and the company we are making payments to are both of no help and have been brushing us off and we are urgently needing help. 

We are requesting for our situation to be reviewed and investigated because we would be horrified if this was happening to others as well and feel it is only right to report what has happened to me and my family. We are now in a horrible payment and fraudulent program and would like this to be rectified as soon as possible. The lender knowingly forced us into a fraudulent situation. We have not been able to get anywhere with the lender or the investor and this is why we are reaching out to the CFPB for help because this is the only other hope we have in getting some resolution to this tragic situation. 

Thank you,

Consumer complaint narrative:
I purchased my first condo in XX/XX/XXXX. The building has a Mills Act contract, so owners have the benefit of greatly reduced property taxes. My annual property taxes should be close to {$6000.00}, but in actuality, they're closer to {$1500.00} with the tax reduction. But it was explained to me that until property tax bills were issued to me, my loan provider had no way of knowing how much less Id actually be paying. So when I closed, I was required to fund my escrow account with a much higher amount than I would ever really need. But I knew Id eventually get some of it back once the loan provider could see what my bills actually would be. My mortgage broker advised me to contact the loan service company XXXX Rocket Mortgage ) once I received my first property tax bill so they could do an escrow analysis so that I could hopefully get a refund and reduce my future monthly escrow payments. 

I received my first tax bill in the beginning of XXXX. Ill note that it seemed a little odd to me that it was addressed to the previous owner, but I didn't think that mattered, as it was a tax bill for XXXX, and it clearly showed the property taxes that were owed. By this point, I knew that my escrow account was scheduled for analysis in XX/XX/XXXX, but I was hoping to speed up the process by a month or XXXX, so I called Rocket Mortgage. The man I spoke to was very helpful. He suggested I upload the bill and then call back in a few days to make sure it had been received. At that point, they could request an escrow analysis. And then life happened and before I knew it, it was XXXX and I hadn't had a chance to call back yet. In that time, I had received another tax bill that was actually in my name, and had the same amounts due. But I didn't think that it would matter, since it was all the same info, minus my name, so I filed the bill away and forgot about it. In that time, Rocket Mortgage had also made my first property tax payment, so they clearly had accurate data on how much I was actually paying. 

At the beginning of XXXX, I finally called Rocket Mortgage back. They confirmed that they had received the property tax bill that Id uploaded and that they would move forward with an escrow analysis. The woman I spoke to, XXXX, estimated that I'd have a refund by the end of the month and reduced monthly escrow payments by XXXX. She mentioned nothing about the property tax bill I sent having the name of the previous owner. 

XXXX turned to XXXX, and I had seen no progress on the Rocket Mortgage website regarding my escrow account. On XX/XX/XXXX, I called again to check in and spoke to XXXX. He confirmed that they were still researching my property tax situation, which at this point was a little confusing to me why they had to research. They clearly had my property tax payment info, since they had already made XXXX payment in XXXX. But I didn't question him further on the topic. He also confirmed that my annual analysis was scheduled for XXXX, so it basically was going to coincide with the research that was already happening. He said to give it another week or so. He mentioned nothing about the tax bill I had submitted in XXXX having the name of the previous owner. 

On XX/XX/XXXX, I finally saw that my escrow analysis had been completed. Yay! I was getting a refund... but not as big as I had been expecting And when I started looking at the actual report, I realized that my monthly escrow payments were not changing. And the amount they were estimating I'd pay in property taxes had not changed at all. Now I was really confused. Even if I hadn't uploaded a copy of my property tax bill to them, they had paid my property tax bill in XXXX, so they clearly were getting information directly from my county on how much to pay. And if they had that info, how could they still think that my taxes would still be just shy of {$6000.00}?? 

I called Rocket Mortgage that day and talked to XXXX. It was a very confusing conversation. She seemed to be saying that they had no evidence that my taxes would be less, and therefore I had to wait another year for another analysis for things to be figured out. This is when I started to get angry. She was basically telling me that on top of Rocket Mortgage holding onto thousands of dollars of excess money in my escrow account, I would be required to pay hundreds of dollars more per month for another year until Rocket Mortgage could figure it out. This was completely contradictory to everything Id been told before. And it also seemed not legal. From the little that I understand about Escrow accounts, there are laws in place that limit how much can be held in an escrow account. But by the end, it seemed that the issue was that I had submitted the property tax bill with the previous owner 's name. Which, again, confused me because Rocket had already paid my property tax bill in XXXX, so they could already see that my payments were going to be much less than they had been estimating. I told XXXX that I would upload the proper bill with my name that evening. She said she would call me in a day or so to follow up. 

In retrospect, yes, it logically makes sense that I should have not sent in the bill with the previous owner 's name because her taxes wouldn't necessarily correspond to what I would owe. But this is the first property I have purchased, and I'm learning. I don't know everything. And Rocket Mortgage had multiple chances to inform me that they needed the bill with my name. Yet it wasnt until I talked to XXXX, more than XXXX months after I had first initially contacted them, and after the analysis had been completed, that I was told that they didnt have what they needed. 

I uploaded the proper bill that evening. It was a holiday weekend, so I called the following Tuesday, XX/XX/XXXX, to confirm that they had received the bill. The man I spoke to, XXXX, said they had received it. I missed a call from XXXX the next day XX/XX/XXXX. She left a message saying that she had an update and if I called back, anyone I talked to would have the update. I called and spoke to XXXX. He could find no record of a note from XXXX about an update. He said hed get in touch with her and give me a call back. He called me the next day, XX/XX/XXXX. He said that the update was simply that they had received the property tax bill. All looked good. And they were moving forward with an additional escrow analysis. I asked him what the timeframe would be for the process. He said it would take XXXX business days, so Id probably hear back the following week. 

I didnt hear anything the entire following week, and on XX/XX/XXXX, I received an email saying that my loan was being transferred to XXXX XXXX  XXXX I called Rocket Mortgage the following Monday for an update and spoke with XXXX. I was hoping he would say that everything would be figured out before the loan was transferred. But instead, he basically told me that Id have to deal with it with XXXX. He reiterated that an analysis would take XXXX business days, so even if they started the analysis today it wouldnt get done in time. So, apparently, despite XXXX different people telling me the analysis had started, it had in fact not been started at all. And now I was stuck having to start the whole process over again with a new loan servicer. 

I fully understand that I did not provide the correct document in the beginning, but Rocket  Mortgage had many chances to inform me that they needed a different document. And furthermore, I am still very confused about how Rocket Mortgage can still think my property taxes would be close to {$6000.00} for the year when the last payment they made for me in XX/XX/XXXX was around {$750.00}. Something that should have taken weeks has now dragged out into months. In the meantime, Rocket Mortgage has been holding onto an excess amount of money in my escrow account. And Ive had to pay hundreds of dollars more for XXXX, and now probably XXXX too since I dont have high hopes that XXXX will be any quicker in figuring this all out. This has been a very frustrating experience. And of course Rocket Mortgage doesnt have to deal with it anymore since my loan has been transferred. So I figured the only thing I could do at this point is write up this complaint.

sect 501.37 1 ) Every lender of money, whether a natural person or an artificial entity, whose loans are secured by a mortgage on real estate located within the state and who receives funds incidental thereto or in connection therewith for the payment of property taxes or hazard insurance premiums when the funds are held in escrow by or on behalf of the lender, shall promptly pay the taxes or insurance premiums when the taxes or premiums become due and adequate escrow funds are deposited, so that the maximum tax discount available may be obtained with regard to the taxable property and so that insurance coverage on the property does not lapse. 
( 2 ) If an escrow account for the taxes or insurance premiums is deficient, the lender shall notify the property owner within 15 days after the lender receives the notification of taxes due from the county tax collector or receives the notification from the insurer that a premium is due. 
( 3 ) ( a ) If the lender, as a result of neglect, fails to pay any tax or insurance premium when the tax or premium is due and there are sufficient escrow funds on deposit to pay the tax or premium, and if the property owner suffers a loss as a result of this failure, then the lender is liable for the loss ; except, however, that with respect to any loss which would otherwise have been insured, the extent of the liability shall not exceed the coverage limits of any insurance policy which has lapsed. 
( b ) If the lender violates paragraph ( a ) and the premium payment is not more than 90 days overdue, the insurer shall reinstate the insurance policy, retroactive to the date of cancellation, and the lender shall reimburse the property owner for any penalty or fees imposed by the insurer and paid by the property owner for purposes of reinstating the policy. 
( c ) If the lender violates paragraph ( a ) and the premium payment is more than 90 days overdue or if the insurer refuses to reinstate the insurance policy, the lender shall pay the difference between the cost of the previous insurance policy and a new, comparable insurance policy for a period of 2 years. If the lender refuses, the lender is liable for the reasonable attorneys fees and costs of the property owner for a violation of this section. 
( 4 ) At the expiration of the annual accounting period, the lender shall issue to the property owner an annual statement of the escrow account.
